extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotle / students of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Aristotle's evaluative principles concerning Pleasure, Self-Mastery, and the nature and kinds of Friendship from Books VII–VIII of the Nicomachean Ethics. Focuses on what counts as good/bad pleasure and the conditions and species of friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low/noxious pleasures are not-good
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Pleasures of this class are actings of a low nature, whether congenital as in brutes, or acquired by custom as in low bad men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasures that are 'low' (either congenital or acquired by bad custom) are judged not-good. Violent or excessive pleasures pursued by those who can relish no others create violent thirsts for themselves; harmless violent pleasures are not faulted, but harmful ones are 'bad and low.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial pleasures (cures) are less good than original health
rubrics_metrics.description: Others are in the nature of cures, cures that is of some deficiency; now of course it is better to have [the healthy state] originally than that it should accrue afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasures that result from curing a deficiency are pleasant as results but are considered inferior to having the healthy state originally. Such 'result' pleasures are distinct from pleasures that naturally accompany a perfected state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures that perfect natural states are good
rubrics_metrics.description: But some Pleasures result when natural states are being perfected: these therefore are good as a matter of result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a pleasure accompanies the perfection of a natural state (i.e., actualization of a sound part of the constitution), it is good as a result. Aristotle distinguishes pleasures as remedial results versus those that naturally express a pleasant nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures unconnected with pain do not admit of excess
rubrics_metrics.description: But those Pleasures which are unconnected with Pains do not admit of excess: i.e. such as belong to objects which are naturally pleasant and not merely as a matter of result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Pleasant naturally" means pleasures that put into action a nature which is pleasant; these are not subject to excess in the same way as violent or remedial pleasures. The complexity of human nature prevents one thing being always pleasant to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure often drives out Pain and can undermine self-mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure drives out Pain; not only such Pleasure as is directly contrary to Pain but even any Pleasure provided it be strong: and this is how men come to be utterly destitute of Self-Mastery, i.e. low and bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong pleasures (especially violent ones) can displace pain and lead some persons to lack self-control; this explains why certain pleasures are morally suspect when they lead to uncontrolled appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship requires mutual kindly feelings known to both parties
rubrics_metrics.description: To complete the idea of Friendship, then, it is requisite that they have kindly feelings towards one another, and wish one another good from one of the aforementioned causes, and that these kindly feelings should be mutually known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere kindly disposition toward another (even without reciprocity) is 'kindly-disposed' but not full Friendship; mutual recognition of the goodwill is necessary to constitute friendship proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: There are three species of Friendship (utility, pleasure, goodness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The species then of Friendship are three, in number equal to the objects of it... since in the line of each there may be 'mutual affection mutually known.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendships correspond to their motivating object: utility (useful), pleasure (pleasant), and the good/virtue (perfect). Each has distinct motives, features, and stability; Aristotle treats them as distinct species rather than mere degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship of utility: result-based and liable to dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: They whose motive is utility have no Friendship for one another really, but only in so far as some good arises to them from one another... Such Friendships are of course very liable to dissolution if the parties do not continue alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility friendships exist insofar as advantage accrues; they commonly dissolve when advantage ceases. They are associated with certain life stages or roles (e.g., merchants, some older people) and often lack intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship of pleasure: based on mutual enjoyment; changeable (common among the young)
rubrics_metrics.description: They whose motive is pleasure ... have Friendship for men of easy pleasantry, not because they are of a given character but because they are pleasant to themselves... The young are much given up to Love; this passion being... based on pleasure: for which cause they conceive Friendships and quickly drop them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure-based friendships depend on present pleasures and are therefore often short-lived and changeable. They prompt intimate society and are frequent among the young whose pleasures shift quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect friendship (based on goodness) wishes good for friend's sake and is permanent
rubrics_metrics.description: That then is perfect Friendship which subsists between those who are good and whose similarity consists in their goodness: for these men wish one another's good in similar ways; in so far as they are good (and good they are in themselves)... the Friendship between these men continues to subsist so long as they are good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect friendship is disinterested: friends wish good to each other for the other's sake, not for pleasure or profit. Such friendships combine mutual usefulness and pleasure abstractedly, are intense, rare, and require time and intimacy to form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is more stable when the same results accrue to both from the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships are most permanent when the same result accrues to both from one another, pleasure, for instance; and not merely so but from the same source...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocity in both outcome and source (both derive the same benefit/pleasure from the same cause) strengthens permanence; asymmetrical sources (e.g., lover vs. beloved) are more fragile over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship requires some degree of equality or proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality, then, and similarity are a tie to Friendship, and specially the similarity of goodness... the better man, or the more profitable, and so forth, should be the object of a stronger feeling than he himself entertains, because when the feeling of Friendship comes to be after a certain rate then equality in a certain sense is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship between unequal parties should maintain a proportionate feeling to create functional equality. Extreme disparities of goodness, prosperity, or station typically preclude genuine friendship (e.g., gods vs. men, kings vs. very insignificant persons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship among unequal roles differs in kind (parent-child, ruler-ruled, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another form of Friendship, that, namely, in which the one party is superior to the other; as between father and son, elder and younger, husband and wife, ruler and ruled. These also differ one from another... because the work, and therefore the excellence, of each of these is different, and different therefore are the causes of their feeling Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different superior-inferior relationships produce different friendship feelings and expectations; permanence and equity require each party to render what is due according to their role (e.g., children to parents, parents to offspring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance and lack of intercourse weaken Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance has in itself no direct effect upon Friendship, but only prevents the acting it out: yet, if the absence be protracted, it is thought to cause a forgetfulness even of the Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Living together and frequent intercourse are characteristic of strong friendships because friends share pleasurable activity and assist one another; long absences can erode the state of friendship by preventing acts that instantiate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good men are stable friends and resist calumny
rubrics_metrics.description: The Friendship of the good is alone superior to calumny; it not being easy for men to believe a third person respecting one whom they have long tried and proved: there is between good men mutual confidence...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendships grounded in virtue produce mutual trust and confidence; they are robust against slander and suspicion, unlike friendships of pleasure or profit which lack such stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being the object of Friendship differs from entertaining the sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship stands rather in the entertaining, than in the being the object of, the sentiment... entertaining the sentiment is like a feeling, but Friendship itself like a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can take delight in being regarded as a friend (the object) without reciprocating the state of friendship; true friendship is a moral state involving active wishing of the other's good, not merely being the recipient of goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect friendship is rare and requires time and intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rare it is probable Friendships of this kind will be, because men of this kind are rare. Besides, all requisite qualifications being presupposed, there is further required time and intimacy... men cannot know one another till they have eaten the requisite quantity of salt together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect friendships require both virtuous characters and proven experience of one another; quick interchange of friendly acts may indicate a wish to be friends but not genuine friendship until proven fit and mutually known.

rubrics_metrics.name: People may have multiple friends for different purposes (useful vs. pleasant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men in power are often seen to make use of several distinct friends: for some are useful to them and others pleasurable, but the two are not often united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is common and acceptable to have different friends serving different ends (utility vs. pleasure); only rarely do the same persons combine pleasantness and goodness or usefulness for honourable purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendships based on profit commonly arise from contrary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Friendship based on motives of profit is thought to be most of all formed out of contrary elements: the poor man, for instance, is thus a friend of the rich, and the ignorant of the man of information...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profit friendships often involve exchange of complementary goods or services (poor-rich, ignorant-informed, lover-beloved). Such friendships are essentially transactional and liable to be ridiculous if one party exaggerates equality of feeling.
